slides.heading: Cycle In Graph
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Graphs
slides.narration: Let's solve Cycle In Graph, a medium graphs problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Directed graph as adjacency list; does it contain a cycle? 3-colour DFS.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Directed graph as adjacency list; does it contain a cycle? 3-colour DFS.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: A cycle exists if depth-first search meets a node that's still on the current recursion stack.
slides.narration: A cycle exists if depth-first search meets a node that's still on the current recursion stack.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: from each node, DFS to see if you return → O(V·(V+E))
Single DFS with three colours → O(V + E)
Alternative: Kahn's topological sort fails ⇒ cycle
slides.narration: Running a separate search from every node to see if it returns is slow. One depth-first search with three colours finds a cycle in linear time: an edge to a node that's still on the recursion stack is a back edge. Kahn's algorithm is an alternative.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 3. Edge to a grey node is a back edge, a cycle
slides.narration: Step by step. First, colour nodes white, grey, black. Second, grey means on the stack. Third, edge to a grey node is a back edge, a cycle.

slides.narration: Enter node 0 and colour it grey, meaning it's on the current path.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Edge 2 → 0 hits a grey node → cycle
slides.narration: Node 2 has an edge to 0, which is still grey, on the current path. That's a back edge, so there's a cycle.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We colour every node white, then DFS from each unvisited node. DFS marks the node grey, returns true if any neighbour is grey or if recursing into a white neighbour finds a cycle, and marks the node black when finished.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of v plus e. Space is O of v.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Visited ≠ on-stack: finished (black) nodes are safe
Disconnected graphs: start DFS from every node
slides.narration: Don't confuse visited with on the stack: reaching a finished node isn't a cycle. Self-loops count, and you must start from every unvisited node to cover disconnected parts.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: undirected graphs (ignore the parent edge)
slides.narration: Explain the three colours clearly. For undirected graphs, the rule changes: ignore the edge back to the parent.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: A cycle exists if depth-first search meets a node that's still on the current recursion stack.
slides.narration: To recap Cycle In Graph: A cycle exists if depth-first search meets a node that's still on the current recursion stack. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
